analysis.one_liner: Requires pharmacy benefit managers to disclose drug-pricing data and pass all manufacturer rebates to health plans.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote and died in the House Energy and Commerce Committee's Health Subcommittee when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: Pharmacy benefit managers — the middlemen that negotiate drug prices for employer and insurance plans — would have to report what they pay pharmacies, what manufacturers pay them in rebates and fees, and what they charge plans, in machine-readable reports to plan sponsors twice a year. They would have to hand 100% of manufacturer rebates and discounts back to the health plans, offer contracts where the plan is not charged more for a drug than the pharmacy was paid (ending "spread pricing"), and face civil fines of up to $10,000 a day for hiding information or filing false reports. Employers and plan sponsors could audit rebate contracts. The bill never moved past its committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Employers and other plan sponsors who pay for health coverage, and the enrollees on those plans. Today, plans often cannot see how much of a drug's list price is captured by the PBM in rebates, fees, and the gap between what a pharmacy is paid and what the PBM bills the plan. The bill would put that data in the sponsor's hands, return all manufacturer rebates to the plan (money that could lower premiums or cost-sharing), and ban charging the plan more than the pharmacy received without the plan's express permission.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Employers and workers on health plans

how_it_helps.text: Requires twice-yearly machine-readable reports to plan sponsors covering drug-by-drug utilization, gross and net spending, rebates and fees received, out-of-pocket enrollee spending, and the rationale for formulary placement choices.
Requires PBMs and insurers to remit 100% of manufacturer rebates, fees, and discounts to the health plan within 120 days, fully disclosed and subject to plan audits of the rebate contracts.

Bans "spread pricing" — charging a plan or enrollee more for a drug than the pharmacy was paid — unless the plan sponsor expressly permits it, and requires extra quarterly reporting when a PBM steers fills to a pharmacy it owns.
Attaches civil monetary penalties of $10,000 per day for failing to report or engaging in spread pricing, and up to $100,000 per item for knowingly providing false information.

analysis.who_pays: Pharmacy benefit managers and the insurer parent companies that own them, which would give up rebate retention, spread-pricing margin, and the confidentiality of their manufacturer deals. Health insurers and PBMs would also bear the cost of building the reporting systems, some of which could be passed back to plans in fees.
analysis.who_pays_short: Pharmacy benefit managers and their insurer owners

drawbacks.text: Transparency alone does not lower anyone's drug price. The bill relies on employers and plan sponsors using the new data to renegotiate; if they do not, enrollees see no direct benefit.

The bill does not require the reports to be made public: it explicitly lets insurers and PBMs place reasonable restrictions on public disclosure, and the reports go to the plan sponsor, not to patients, so enrollees would not necessarily see the data themselves.

PBMs may continue to keep "bona fide service fees" from manufacturers, so long as those fees are disclosed and not tied to a drug's price or formulary placement — meaning some manufacturer payments remain in PBM hands.
The compliance and reporting burden falls on insurers and PBMs, and some of that cost could be passed back to the plans they serve.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core bargain is real: self-funded employers — who cover a large share of insured Americans — would finally see where their drug dollars go and could audit the contracts, and rebate pass-through directly shifts money from PBM margins back to plans. The weaknesses are that it is a disclosure bill rather than a price-control bill, patients themselves do not get the data, and PBM service fees remain. On balance it is a modest, well-designed transparency measure whose main cost falls on the middlemen, not the public.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Health Subcommittee, where it sat without a hearing, markup, or vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Kurt Schrader, a Democrat from Oregon, introduced the bill on December 4, 2019, joined by Republican Rep. Greg Gianforte of Montana as the bill's sole cosponsor.
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce; the next day it was referred to the Health Subcommittee. That was the last action ever taken on it.
No hearing, markup, floor vote, or Senate companion action followed before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, so the bill died in subcommittee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pharmacy benefit managers and their insurer owners kept their rebate retention, spread pricing, and confidential manufacturer deals untouched. Employers and patients gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Pharmacy benefit managers kept the status quo

for.name: Rep. Kurt Schrader
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and became its sole Democratic sponsor.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral, sent it to the Health Subcommittee, and never held a hearing or markup, leaving it to die when the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was bipartisan in sponsorship — one Democrat and one Republican — but only two members in the whole House backed it, so party positions were never tested with a vote.

industries.industry: Pharmacy benefit managers (CVS Caremark, Express Scripts, OptumRx and peers)
industries.note: The bill targets the core of the PBM business model: rebates the PBM keeps rather than passes through, spread pricing that charges plans more than pharmacies were paid, and confidentiality of manufacturer deals. It would also expose the share of fills steered to PBM-owned pharmacies. Under the bill these practices are penalized and much of the revenue is returned to plans.

Insurers that own PBMs (Aetna-CVS, Cigna-Express Scripts, UnitedHealth-OptumRx) would lose the rebate and spread-pricing revenue that flows through those arms and would fund the reporting systems. Their core insurance business gets disclosure obligations but no direct revenue cut.

Employers that fund their own health plans would receive detailed twice-yearly pricing and rebate reports and the right to audit rebate contracts, giving them leverage to negotiate lower drug costs — savings that flow to the plan and its enrollees.

The ban on charging plans more than the pharmacy was paid removes the spread-pricing margin PBMs currently capture at the pharmacy's expense, and the reporting on PBM-owned pharmacies addresses steering away from independent drugstores.

Manufacturers would have to report copay-assistance spending and would see their rebate deals disclosed to plan sponsors and opened to audit, but the bill leaves the rebate system itself in place and lets PBMs keep bona fide service fees.
